title.narrative: NIHR Global Health Research Short Placement Award for Research Collaboration (GHR SPARC) Award- Ms. Antoinette Buhle Ndweni NIHR GHR SPARC-R3-006

description.narrative: I am undertaking this research as part my PhD training under the NIHR GHR Group on HIVassociated Fungal Infections (IMPRINT) to develop my skills as a health economic modeller and researcher. I’m mainly excited to be working on research that will improve the quality of life of patients living with advanced HIV disease, while also reducing the mortality rates from HIVrelated fungal infections through early screening and treatment. The aim of the placement is to add to my taught master’s studies, by providing more insight on modelling approaches when simulating disease pathways in advanced HIV patients and related fungal infections when working with data from the EFFECT clinical trial (partly nested within IMPRINT). The placement will take place while I attend two advanced training courses offered in-person by the University of York’s Centre for Health Economics. These will help to bridge economic evaluation knowledge gaps I need to gear me up for building de novo economic models as part of my PhD training. The impact made by the SPARC placement can be measured through my increased capabilities to confidently and independently build statistically accurate economic models in HIV disease. The expectation is for the additional skills learned through the placement to contribute to producing health outcomes that inform public health policy in South Africa and beyond. My hopes are for the longer-term benefits of this placement to be seen through the World Health Organization making recommendations for ODA-eligible countries external of the EFFECT clinical trial, these countries would in turn adopt the early screening and treatment of AHD-related fungal infections within their health policy – ultimately saving lives at an exponential level.

activity-date.narrative: The GHR SPARC placement enabled me to attend the online ‘Decision Modelling for Health Economic Evaluation – Advanced course’ delivered by the University of York in partnership with the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. This was followed by a 2-week in person visit in the UK where I was hosted by the University of York (UoY). I engaged with the UoY faculty members on my NIHR GHR IMPRINT PhD research project. The meetings I had with the placement host Professor Simon Walker prior to and during the UK visit enabled me to flesh out how to better approach the decision analytic modelling of HIV-associated fungal infections in advanced HIV patients. Professor Walker arranged for me to present an informal seminar that was attended by both UoY’s Centre for Health Economics (CHE) and other visiting faculty. He also set up meetings with other faculty members who have worked on health economic methodology that would be of relevance to my PhD research. This enabled me to ask these experts about any challenges I had with al modelling approaches for my PhD objectives. While in York I attended the in-person ‘Statistical Methods in Economic Evaluation for HTA (SMEEHTA) – Advanced course’ offered by UoY. This training provided a great platform to network with other health analysts across the world and to learn about their research projects and /or health economics related industry work they are involved in. Sharing the office with research researchers at UoY’s CHE enabled me to get a bit of a glimpse into the projects they were working on and to understand the reason UK based institutions has an interest in research projects within low-to middle-income settings – which is mainly for research and capacity building.

recipient-country.narrative: The awardee of the SPARC award is based in South Africa, currently studying for her PhD in Health Economics at the University of Cape Town.
